en: Once upon a time, a certain sovereign of monkeys, the most excellent among speakers, summoned his own people, convened an assembly of his kin, and spoke these words: (1)
O elders of the monkey lineage, it is indeed known to you that those great men born of our family were renowned throughout the three worlds for their heroism, valor, and learning. (2)
Who in this world does not know that heroic monkey named Sugrīva, who was chosen as a companion by the prince of Kosala for the sake of finding his beloved? (3)
In what lineage was that Vālī born, who—pierced by the joy of the Raghus while hiding—dragged the Lord of Laṅkā, whose power was renowned for making Mount Kailāsa tremble, like a mere worm? (4)

In which lineage was that illustrious Hanumān born—he who earned renown by leaping across the ocean, whose majesty shone through the burning of the city of Laṅkā, and who was an expert in the new grammar? (5)
"O elders of the monkey lineage, tell us: where was this Nala born in that family by which the bridge, famous here as the *Setu*, was fastened across the ocean by the bull of the Raghus?"
What is the use of enumerating all these great ones who have been the ornaments of our lineage?
I shall say something intended for discussion; let the virtuous listen closely and reflect upon it. (7)
What indeed is lacking among us such that we would be inferior to the human race? Or what excellence shines forth among humans by which the human class might be considered superior? (8)
Having thus uttered these words full of meaning, that eloquent monkey became silent;
with a mind steady and slow due to the pride of his own oratory, he gazed for a moment all around the assembly.
Of the monkeys, whose faces were blooming with words of self-exaltation, by means of various graceful movements of their limbs.
Encouraged by this, that king of monkeys was delighted and again spoke these steady words.
Therefore, O venerable ones, reflect today upon the dharmas shown by the various branches [of our tradition]:
why should that which is appropriate for the human race not also apply to one born of our own family? (11)
Even though this tradition has long been dormant, it must certainly be preserved by you;
for if the Dharma were to perish, the claim that we have become deer would surely become firmly established among us. (12)
Therefore, those who would endure this temporary affliction should fix their minds upon the path of the eternal Dharma;
since tomorrow shall be the Ekādaśī, fast then and first establish yourselves in righteousness.
Having sprinkled the nectar into the ears of the monkeys, the wheel-turning monarch, rejoicing at their many visible signs of satisfaction, ceased [his pouring].
He then proclaimed his love-filled worship, which was dense with chirping sounds and visible through various leaps. 14.
Having made their resolve regarding the fast, they departed with joy, delighted by their shared human experience.
Then, having awakened at dawn and purified their bodies by bathing in river water,
they placed the delightful Rāma in their hearts and resolved to observe a fast.
Then, as they stood silently for half a moment, intent on gazing at one another—
Even in his body, as if in his heart, a restlessness arose; for who can transcend his own nature?

(17) Having yawned, shaken off [the dust], stretching out his hand, shifting his foot, and twisting his body, a certain monkey at last broke the silence by licking the tip of his tail, unable to endure the itching. (18)
"Without doubt, this vow of great merit must now be observed by the great ones;
nevertheless, it appears that our breaking of the fast will take place tomorrow for those dwelling at the foot of the Jambu tree.
Thus spoke that monkey, in words befitting his own character, while they rejoiced in response.
Due to their satisfaction at the destruction of the affliction of maintaining a steady posture, others, being monkeys, cried out, "They are equal! || 20 ||

"So be it; what is the harm in staying here? If our limbs are afflicted by the exhaustion of vows and fasting, we shall likely not have the strength to travel from here toward the trees in the morning. (21)
Having thus resolved, the monkeys leaped freely from the bank of the river and, moving about,
reached the base of a jambu tree where they sat down, forming a row.
Remaining thus, they somehow passed some moments with glances fixed momentarily and looks cast in all directions, and by scratching themselves most rapidly. || 23 ||
Then, a certain monkey of undiminished courage rose up and said to the leaders of the monkeys:
"If we climb a tree and lie down there, what harm could possibly come to us? (24)

Accepting that there would be no violation whatsoever of their vow in that situation, those monkey-leaders, observers of the vow, climbed the tree and remained poised upon its spreading branches. (25)
There, for those who remained silent on one side, whose exertion was doubled by their persistence,
and who were incessantly occupied with meditation on fasting, every single moment appeared as long as an eon.
Beholding the fruits—succulent with juice and falling noisily from tree branches shaken by the wind—their minds became agitated as saliva flowed from their mouths. (27)
While everyone’s own desires— which follow after their fruits— were being shattered like blades of grass and their silence broken,
one person, regaining his composure, spoke out with his whole heart, as if expressing his own inner intent.
Indeed, a pair of bellows has been fashioned for our cheeks by the all-knowing Creator;
let us fill them today with faultless fruits, so that tomorrow we shall have no distress from the search for fruit. (29)

"So be it," they said; then those foremost of monkeys, having leapt up and wandered among the branches and sub-branches, quickly filled the caves of their mouths with fruits that were unripe yet beautiful in their full ripeness.
After that, there was nothing further to be done here, nor anything else to be communicated to one another;
therefore, wandering at will, the monkeys carried off our writing-stylus as we were indeed writing. (35)
